risc-v-core.title: RISC-V-Core
risc-v-core.subtitle: 32-bit RISC-V core implementing an RV32I instruction subset, with SystemVerilog RTL, directed and constrained-random verification, and a SKY130 synthesis and physical design flow.
risc-v-core.markdown:
32-bit RISC-V core implementing an RV32I instruction subset, with SystemVerilog RTL, directed and constrained-random verification, and a SKY130 synthesis and physical design flow.

## Overview
### About the Project
This repository contains the files for a 32-bit CPU core I designed based on a subset of the RISC-V ISA. I have worked through the full RTL-to-GDS flow, from digital design to design verification to physical design. The final chip core has an area of about 800,000 microns squared, with a 2:1 aspect ratio (1,271.95 microns x 635.975 microns). The chip features two 1024x32 SRAM macros (ISRAM and DSRAM), and 6,798 standard cells.

![CPU Layout Image](Docs/Images/CPUAfterHSOptimizations.PNG)

### Why I Built This
This project was made as part of the onboarding process for the Georgia Tech SiliconJackets club. Additionally, this project taught me the fundamental skills needed to enter the world of VLSI design: digital design, design verification, and physical design. This is a field that I have grown increasingly interested in recently, and I hope to create more complex designs in the future.

### Attributions
As this project was done as part of the SiliconJackets onboarding process, some of the files in this repo were provided by them. These include
- SRAM Macro/Memory Controler
- Some verification skeleton code
- Certain physical design config files
- Makefiles
- Register File

## Project Status
This project is still actively being improved. I am currently working on adding instruction pipelining to increase the clock frequency.

## Repository Structure
| Folder | Details |
| ------ | ------- |
| RTL | Contains the RTL for the CPU, memory controller, and chip_top. Does not contain the SRAM macro due to licensing restrictions. Written in SystemVerilog |
| Verification | Contains an initial and final testplan outlining the full verification process of this design. Also includes a testbench with a driver, monitor, scoreboard, sequencer, and reference model. |
| Physical Design | Contains configuration and flow scripts for synthesis and place/route. THe outputs of synthesis and place/route have not been included to avoid publishing licensed content. |
| Docs | Contains supplementary materials such as images of the chip and its architecture |

## CPU Architecture
![System Architecture Image](Docs/Images/SystemArchitecture.png)
![CPU Architecture Image](<Docs/Images/CPUArchitecture.png>)

## Supported Instructions
The following Subset of the RISC-V ISA has been implemented

- `addi`: addition with a signed immediate
- `add`: register-register add
- `sub`: register-register subtract
- `lw`: load word from data SRAM using an immediate offset
- `sw`: store word to data SRAM using an immediate offset
- `beq` against x0: branch if zero
- `sll`: left logical shift
- `srl`: right logical shift
- `ebreak`: halt the CPU

## Verification
![Verification Architecture Image](Docs/Images/VerificationArchitecture.png)

## Physical Design
The physical design uses the SJapr environment provided by SiliconJackets. The flow utilizes Synopsys Design Compiler and Cadence Innovus.

## Results
The following results describe the current physical implementation. Functional verification is ongoing.

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Core dimensions | 1,271.95 × 635.975 µm |
| Core area | 808,928 µm² (0.809 mm²) |
| Aspect ratio | 2:1 |
| SRAM capacity | Two 1024 × 32-bit macros: 4 KiB instruction memory and 4 KiB data memory |
| Standard-cell count | 6,798 |
| Core utilization | 46.925087 |
| Target clock period | 5 ns |
| Post-route setup WNS / TNS | -1946.496627 ns |

### Verification Results
Directed and constrained-random tests check instruction execution, register state, memory accesses, and interface behavior against a reference model.

### DRC/LVS Results
Both DRC and LVS both currently have numerous errors. I am currently in the process of fixing these errors
![DRC Violoations Image](Docs/Images/DRC.png)
![LVS Violations Image](Docs/Images/LVS.png)

### Layout
![CPU layout after optimization](Docs/Images/CPUAfterHSOptimizations.PNG)

## Requirements and External Dependencies

The verification and physical design flows require a Linux environment with licensed EDA tools. These tools and third-party technology files are not distributed with this repository.

### Required Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| GNU Make | Runs the repository’s build targets |
| Python 3 | Generates simulation source links and synthesis file lists |
| Cadence Xcelium | Compiles and runs the SystemVerilog testbench |
| Cadence SimVision | Displays simulation waveforms |
| Cadence IMC | Analyzes simulation coverage |
| Synopsys Design Compiler | Synthesizes the RTL |
| Cadence Innovus | Performs physical implementation |
| Cadence Virtuoso and Pegasus | Support layout inspection and DRC/LVS checks |
| `tcsh` | Runs the physical design environment and launcher scripts |

Verification has been run using **Xcelium 25.03-s003**. Other tool versions have not been confirmed.

Valid licenses and access to the relevant license servers are required. The physical design environment setup contains Georgia Tech-specific paths that must be adapted for other installations.

### SRAM Dependencies

The design uses two `CF_SRAM_1024x32` SRAM instances. Authorized users must obtain the required models and physical views separately.

Place the simulation model at:

```text
RTL/src/CF_SRAM_1024x32.tt_180V_25C.v
```

Place the SRAM physical-design package under:

```text
Physical Design/inputs/CF_SRAM_1024x32/
├── lib/    # Liberty timing models
├── db/     # Compiled timing library
├── lef/    # Physical abstract
└── gds/    # Macro layout
```

LVS additionally requires:

```text
Physical Design/signoff/CF_SRAM_1024x32.cdl
```

Simulation selects the `CF_SRAM_1024x32_macro` model through the `SIM` define. Synthesis uses the `CF_SRAM_1024x32` library cell.

### SKY130 Technology Dependencies

The current scripts expect the following directory structure:

```text
Physical Design/resources/
├── cadence_sky130/
│   ├── sky130_release_0.1.0/
│   └── sky130_scl_9T_0.1.2/
└── synopsys_libs/
```

These directories provide standard-cell timing libraries, physical abstracts, extraction technology, and physical-verification rules. The `synopsys_libs/` directory contains the compiled libraries referenced by the synthesis scripts.

Obtain the exact compatible packages through an authorized provider or institutional installation. A generic SKY130 installation may not match the filenames, cells, or formats expected by this flow.

### Dependency Licensing

External models, libraries, and technology files remain subject to their respective licenses. They are excluded through `.gitignore` and must be installed locally before running the corresponding flows.

## Running the Project

Install the external dependencies described above before running the flows. Execute the following commands on a Linux machine with access to the required EDA tools and licenses.

### Clone the Repository

```sh
git clone https://github.com/JoelBiswas/RISC-V-Core.git
cd RISC-V-Core
```

### Configure the Simulation Environment

On the Georgia Tech server, enter `tcsh` and load Cadence:

```sh
tcsh
source /tools/software/cadence/setup.csh
which xrun
xrun -version
```

Other installations should use their own tool setup scripts.

### Run Verification

From the repository root, run a short simulation:

```sh
make xrun SEED=1 SIM_PLUSARGS="+NUM_RANDOM_PROGRAMS=2 +NUM_RANDOM_XBAR=5"
```

Run the default test suite:

```sh
make xrun SEED=1
```

The default configuration runs the directed tests, 100 random CPU programs, and 30 random external-port transactions. Change `SEED` to exercise another randomized stimulus sequence.

Inspect the simulation log:

```sh
less Verification/sim/behav/WORKSPACE/simulation.log
```

Review the reported errors and completion status; successful compilation alone does not indicate that verification passed.

### View Waveforms

From a graphical session, such as FastX:

```sh
make simvision
```

Waveforms are generated under:

```text
Verification/sim/behav/WORKSPACE/waves.shm/
```

### View Coverage

After running verification:

```sh
make coverage
```

This opens the coverage database in Cadence IMC and applies the exclusions in `Verification/sim/behav/exclusions.vRefine`.

### Run Physical Design

From the repository root:

```sh
cd "Physical Design"
chmod +x scripts/SJapr scripts/helpers/rename_rundir.tcsh
source envsetup
```

The physical design launcher provides these commands:

```sh
SJapr syn     # Synthesis
SJapr apr     # Place and route using existing synthesis outputs
SJapr flow    # Synthesis followed by place and route
```

For interactive execution:

```sh
SJapr syn -i
SJapr apr -i
```

Outputs are generated under `Physical Design/outputs/synthesis/` and `Physical Design/outputs/apr/`.

**Current limitation:** the physical design launcher contains unquoted paths. These must be corrected to support the space in the `Physical Design` directory name before this flow can be treated as reproducible from a fresh clone.

### Clean Simulation Outputs

From the repository root:

```sh
make clean
```

This removes the generated verification workspace, including logs, waveforms, and coverage data. Save any results you want to retain before cleaning.

## Known Limitations and Future Work

### Current Limitations

- **Partial RV32I support:** The core implements `addi`, `add`, `sub`, `lw`, `sw`, `beq`, `sll`, `srl`, and `ebreak`. It does not implement the complete RV32I instruction set.
- **Limited memory:** Instruction and data memories each contain 1024 32-bit words (4 KiB). Memory addresses are reduced to 10-bit word indices; out-of-range accesses are not trapped.
- **Simplified halt behavior:** `ebreak` halts the core rather than entering an architectural exception handler.
- **No instruction pipeline:** The current implementation does not use a staged instruction pipeline.
- **Environment dependencies:** Simulation and physical design require licensed tools and separately obtained SRAM and technology files. Physical design scripts also require path-portability cleanup.

### Future Work

- Add directed regression tests for consecutive loads and stores.
- Introduce instruction pipelining with appropriate data-hazard and branch handling.
- Expand directed and constrained-random testing and document coverage across multiple seeds.
- Extend instruction support toward a more complete RV32I implementation.
- Improve flow portability and automate dependency checks.
- Document reproducible timing, area, and DRC/LVS results for each implementation revision.

## Licensing

This repository combines my original contributions with RTL scaffolding, verification components, and physical design flow files provided through Georgia Tech SiliconJackets.

No repository-wide license is currently granted. Third-party files remain subject to their respective licenses and permissions. Existing copyright and attribution notices are retained.

SRAM models, technology libraries, and other excluded dependencies must be obtained separately through authorized sources. Their exclusion from this repository does not change their licensing terms.

r2d2.title: R2-D2 - A Robotics Journey
r2d2.subtitle: The repository contains the files to build a smaller-scale replica of the R2-D2 droid from the Star Wars universe. The robot can move around and rotate its head, just like in the movies. It is controlled with a PS3 controller. This robotics project was created entirely by me for Hack Club's Highway to Undercity event.
r2d2.markdown:
The repository contains the files to build a smaller-scale replica of the R2-D2 droid from the Star Wars universe. The robot can move around and rotate its head, just like in the movies. It is controlled with a PS3 controller. This robotics project was created entirely by me for Hack Club's Highway to Undercity event. ![IMG_9884 2](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d81d2307-1279-4c8e-9341-65435ef9c383) ![FrontView](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d2635e25-edf3-48ef-bb5e-4dde339aea2e) ## Bill of Materials View the Bill of Materials [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/11K8ikvZwUrrph38blHlkMEm7u3jJ6bzhOUvdLzmd2ws/edit?usp=sharing) ## The Start of the Journey As a **HUGE** Star Wars fan and a robotics enthusiast, I have always thought it would be so cool to have my very own droid, just like the characters from the movies. Through my two years of experience in a FIRST Robotics Competition team (shoutout team 9477), I was able to learn all the skills I would need to build my own droid. When I was introduced to the Hack Club's Highway to Undercity event, which provides high school students with grants to build their dream projects, I knew that this would be the perfect opportunity for me to practice my robotics skills by building a droid. I decided to attempt to build R2-D2, the most iconic droid of the Star Wars Universe. ## About R2-D2 In the movies, R2 has a wide range of abilities such as movement, flight, tasers, a holographic projector, etc. For this project, I decided to focus on two key points of functionality for the droid: movement and head rotation. The robot has three "feet" -- one on the left, one on the right, and one in the center -- each containing a Pololu 12V Motor attached to a wheel. A PS3 controller is used to control the motors and move the droid. A stepper motor is used to control the rotation of R2-D2's head. An ESP32 is used in order to control all of the motor drivers. ## Overview of this Repo **CAD** - Contains the CAD files for the robot, along with images taken in Onshape
**STLs** - Contains files for each part that needs to be 3D printed
**Print** - Contains the 3d print files for the Flashforge Adventurer 5M
**Electrical** - Contains files from KiCAD for the robot's wiring schematics and custom symbols
**Code** - Currently empty but will eventually contain the code for controlling the robot with a PS3 controller.
**JOURNAL.md** - Contains an overview of exactly how I designed and built this robot
**BOM.csv** - A bill of materials for the project in CSV format
## Designing the Robot Click [here](https://cad.onshape.com/documents/fbad7fda3dbb0b1c2d9d3e12/w/7637877b99adba1fcadbcc49/e/54e6ed0ce40017a6b8cdbd53?renderMode=0&uiState=683df9a55faa163533b4a26a) to view the Onshape document for this project. The electronic design was done in KiCAD. ![CAD](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/651a82ae-2b5c-4b16-a0b7-7637af21a6b9) ![Wiring](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/31a58c11-a1ca-4079-acc8-2c377f85e308) ## General Steps for Assembly 1. Print all parts in the STLs folder of this repo. **IMPORTANT NOTE** Print out the BodyButtonFill.stl file six times and print Foot.stl and FootCover.stl three times. 2. Cut out a 5.8" x 6.3" sheet out of 1/8" polycarbonate. 3. Begin assembling the head by hot-gluing the blue pieces into the indents found in the dome. 4. Bolt the top part of the Lazy Susan Bearing to the bottom of the head using M4 bolts. Use the opening in the back of the head to insert the bolts. 5. Hot glue the blue body pieces into the indents found on the body. 6. Bolt the polycarbonate sheet inside the body using 4 M4 bolts. 7. Attach the stepper motor to the inside of the body, on the top face, using 4 M3 bolts. 8. Add the shaft hub to the shaft of the stepper motor. 9. Bolt the shaft hub onto the bottom of the head using 4 M4 bolts. 10. Bolt the bottom of the Lazy Susan Bearing to the top of the body using 4 M4 bolts. 11. Hot glue the blue leg pieces into the indents on the left and right legs. 12. Bolt the left and right legs into the sides of the body using 8 M4 bolts 13. Assemble each of the three feet by placing the 12V motor in the mounting area and placing the wheel on the motor. The wheel should be aligned with the cutout on the bottom of the foot. 14. Attach the left foot, right foot, and center foot to the droid using 2 M4 bolts for each foot. 15. Zip tie each electronic component (1 ESP32, 3 MD10Cs, 1 A4988, 1 12V to 5V Buck Converter, 1 3S LiPo Battery) to the polycarbonate plate using the zip tie mounts 16. Use the wiring schematic in the Electrical folder of this repo to wire the electrical components 17. Attach all the covers using M4 bolts

controller.title: Custom Star Wars RF Controller
controller.subtitle: This repository contains the files to build a custom RF controller in the shape of the Rebel Alliance Logo from Star Wars. The controller consists of two joysticks, six buttons, and is controlled by an ESP32. This project was created entirely by me for Hack Club's Highway to Undercity event. My plan is to test this device by using to control an R2-D2 droid that I designed for the same Hack Club event earlier this summer.
controller.markdown:
This repository contains the files to build a custom RF controller in the shape of the Rebel Alliance Logo from Star Wars. The controller consists of two joysticks, six buttons, and is controlled by an ESP32. This project was created entirely by me for Hack Club's Highway to Undercity event. My plan is to test this device by using to control an [R2-D2 droid that I designed](https://github.com/JoelBiswas/r2d2/tree/main) for the same Hack Club event earlier this summer. ![TopView](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/143f9d58-209f-4534-bad4-7e8569faec4b) ## Bill of Materials View the Bill of Materials [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1eimf_XqeCwkksVUzqHQLZJRxSmD6-AT-35apM8Ljc3Q/edit?usp=sharing) ## The Beginning The idea for this project came after finishing my last project, an R2-D2 droid controlled with a PS3 controller. I thought that it would be interesting to make my own Star Wars-themed RF transmitter to control the droid with. I hoped that this would provide the robot with much greater range than a Bluetooth-based controller. This project felt perfect as I was looking to start a project that expands my electrical skills. My last project was heavily focused on CAD, so I wanted this project to be more focused on wiring schematic and PCB design. Like the droid, this project is also made for Hack Club's Highway to Undercity event, which provides high school students with grants to build their dream projects. ## About the Controller The controller consists of two main parts: the PCB and the case. The PCB consists of an ESP32, two MP1584 buck converters, two KY-023 Joystick Modules, six push buttons, and an nRF24L01+ PA/LNA RF Module. It is powered by a 2S LiPo battery that connects to the PCB using a Deans Connector. The case is 3D-printable and houses the battery and PCB. The two joysticks are labeled LS and RS, and the buttons are labeled A, B, X, Y, 1, and 2. An antenna on the PCB extends up through a hole in the top of the case in order to transmit the RF signals. ## Overview of this Repo **CAD** - Contains the CAD files for the controller, along with images taken from OnShape.
**STLs** - Contains files for each part that needs to be 3D printed
**Print** - Contains the 3d print files for the Flashforge Adventurer 5M
**Electrical** - Contains files from KiCAD for the controller's wiring schematic, custom symbols, custom footprints, and PCB
**Code** - Currently empty but will eventually contain the code for sending RF signals
**JOURNAL.md** - Contains an overview of exactly how I designed and built this robot
**BOM.csv** - A bill of materials for this project in CSV format
## Designing the Robot Click [here](https://cad.onshape.com/documents/af772411fd2681a1311b7be6/w/e5e3a94108ce63d65661e1b4/e/943c3c2dcbac8496e1ce6b2c?renderMode=0&uiState=685208efd1f4554e80aaa1d0) to view the Onshape document for this project. The electronic design was done in KiCAD. ![CAD](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7fa022fe-0a6a-4016-999e-9c11c06d1726) ![PCB](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/af27cc4c-65ff-477b-8f1e-f8973b74a2fd) ## General Steps for Assembly 1. 3D print each of the files in the STLs folder. The case top and bottom should be printed in orange PLA, and the button should be printed six times in black PLA. 2. Place the LiPo battery into the inserts in the case 3. Place the PCB over the battery on the standoffs. Plug the battery into the Deans connector on the PCB 4. Bolt in the top of the case using an M3 bolt on each side 5. Hot glue the 3D printed button onto the PCB buttons

axial-flux.title: Axial-Flux-Motor
axial-flux.subtitle: This repo contains all of the documentation for a custom Axial Flux Motor that I designed and optimized through simulation. In a traditional induction motor, a circular rotor is surrounded by a concentric stator. This geometry leads to bulky motors, as the stator must, by definition, have a larger diameter than the rotor. An axial-flux motor provides the same amount of power but in a much more compact form factor. The motor designed here features one disc-shaped stator sandwiched between two disc-like rotors, all with the same diameter.
axial-flux.markdown: This repo contains all of the documentation for a custom Axial Flux Motor that I designed and optimized through simulation. In a traditional induction motor, a circular rotor is surrounded by a concentric stator. This geometry leads to bulky motors, as the stator must, by definition, have a larger diameter than the rotor. An axial-flux motor provides the same amount of power but in a much more compact form factor. The motor designed here features one disc-shaped stator sandwiched between two disc-like rotors, all with the same diameter. ## Bill of Materials View the Bill of Materials [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1um99Q8psWdzyrdWxXy8ZlloyDOSwwiJQVUL59ZLKdTk/edit?gid=1649894266#gid=1649894266) ## About the Motor The motor uses a dual-rotor, single-stator configuration, with the stator positioned between two rotating magnet discs. Each rotor contains 12 permanent magnets, while the stator consists of 9 copper coils arranged in a three-phase configuration. Placing magnets on both sides of the stator allows the magnetic field to interact with the coils from both directions while keeping the motor compact. Key Specifications Motor Type: Axial Flux Permanent Magnet (AFPM) Configuration: Dual rotor, single stator Nominal Voltage: 12 V Phases: 3 Permanent Magnets: 12 per rotor (24 total) Stator Coils: 9 Coil Wire: 18 AWG copper Turns per Coil: ~70 Rotor Diameter: ~6 in (152 mm) Stator Thickness: ~0.5 in (12.7 mm) Construction: Primarily custom-designed and 3D-printed components The project was built as an exploration of electric motor design, electromagnetism, and mechanical design. The motor's geometry was designed in Onshape, with considerations including magnet placement, coil geometry, rotor-to-stator air gap, bearing and shaft alignment, structural loading, and manufacturability. ## Overview of this Repo CAD - Contains all CAD files for the motor, as well as a link to the public Onshape document Simulation - Contains images of mechanical simulations performed on the motor in Fusion 360 STLs - Contains the STLs for all 3D printable parts Print - Contains sliced files for the FlashForge Adventurer 5M JOURNAL.md - Contains an overview of my process while designing this project BOM.csv - A bill of materials in CSV format

ventilator.title: DIY Ventilator
ventilator.subtitle: The job of a ventilator is to be able to pump out a fixed volume of air at a fixed number of times per minute. These devices became extremely in demand during the 2020 pandemic. Traditional ventilator systems are very expensive, so I attempted to create a cheap, 3D-printable design that uses standard hardware such as nuts and bolts.
ventilator.markdown: ## The Concept The job of a ventilator is to be able to pump out a fixed volume of air at a fixed number of times per minute. These devices became extremely in demand during the 2020 pandemic. Traditional ventilator systems are very expensive, so I attempted to create a cheap, 3D-printable design that uses standard hardware such as nuts and bolts. ## Guide to this Repo This repo contains several top-level files and folders providing documentation for this project **JOURNAL.md** - Contains a log of my progress on this project **BOM.csv** - Detailed Bill of Materials for this project **Demos** - Demo video of the final product **Electrical** - All KiCAD files for this project **CAD** - Contains images of the CAD model, STEP files for each part and assembly, and a link to the public Onshape document for this project **Code** - Contains all firmware for the ventilator **3D Printing** - Contains STL Files for all 3D printable parts, as well as pre-sliced files for the FlashForge Adventurer 5M
